## Intent
Hypothesis: compiler auto-vectorization over per-particle components can approach the streaming ceiling on death-free workloads.

## Layout & approach
The 68 B/p AoS layout offers 32 hot bytes per particle to loop 1 (age+pos+seed+vel, 47%) and 28 to loop 2 (color+pos, 41%); the remaining 53–59% is dead weight dragged through every cacheline fill. No intermediate storage means the death verdict stays in registers, avoiding a second full pass — but the fused integrate+decide+respawn loop still carries the full 68-byte stride, and loop 2's byte-granular render scatter operates on the same AoS stream. With only 47% of loaded bytes actually consumed in loop 1, the effective bandwidth ceiling for useful work is already halved before codegen enters the picture.

## Cache saturation
The ns/p curve is strikingly flat across all regimes. At q=0.01 it rises from 21.0 ns/p (L1d, N=320) to 25.3 ns/p (DRAM, N=10M) — a 20% increase across the entire hierarchy. At q=0.5 it is even flatter: 32.0→32.5. There is no sharp knee at the L1d spill (N≈481), the L2 spill (N≈7710), or the L3 spill (N≈246723). This flatness is diagnostic: if the algo were memory-bound, each spill would produce a step. Instead, per-particle overhead dominates so completely that cache residency barely matters. The dense grid resolves no transition because there is none to resolve.

## Bandwidth
Achieved bandwidth is 2.69–3.23 GB/s against a 12.69 GB/s ceiling — 21–25% of ceiling. The memory floor is 5.359 ns/p; actual cost is 21–32 ns/p, 4–6× above floor. This is frontend-bound, not bandwidth-bound: 63–70% frontend stalls, 0% backend, 0% branch_flush across all profiles. The algo barely outperforms naive scalar: 0.93–0.99× baseline at every N×q point. Against the winner it is 2.8–3.4× slower at q=0.01, narrowing to 1.7–1.9× at q=0.5 — the branchy respawn equalizes somewhat at high death rates but never closes the gap. Cost scales linearly with q (21→25→27.5→32.5 ns/p at large N) with no regime-dependent transition, confirming the bottleneck is instruction count, not memory.

## Assembly
Only 16 of 345 instructions are vectorized (4.6%). Loop 1 uses `vmovups` for the 16-byte position load and `vmulps`/`vaddps`/`vinsertps`/`vshufps` for a partial position update, but drops to scalar `vmulss`/`vaddss` for age and velocity, with 14 conditional branches and a `call` to spawn on death. Loop 2 is entirely scalar: `vucomiss` depth tests, `vcvttss2si` pixel conversion, then byte-granular scatter via `movzx`/`add`/`cmp`/`cmovae`/`strb` — 16 byte stores per iteration across 195 instructions and 21 branches. The 63–70% frontend stall is explained by these long, branchy iteration bodies that defeat the decoders; the partial vectorization in loop 1 cannot compensate for loop 2's scalar scatter.

## Verdict
Refuted — 0.93–0.99× of naive baseline and 2.4–3.4× slower than the winner at q=0.01, sustaining only 21–25% of the streaming ceiling (2.69–3.23 GB/s vs 12.69) with 4–6× headroom above the memory floor. The mechanism is frontend starvation: 16/345 vector instructions, a scalar byte-scatter render loop, and 63–70% frontend stalls show that auto-vectorization never materialized on this AoS layout, and the bottleneck is instruction delivery, not memory bandwidth, at every death rate and cache regime.
